title: Stock Market Crash: Why Monthly Investors Get a Sale
description:
What does a stock market crash mean if you invest every month? In our simple illustration, a fund falls from $100 to $50 and only climbs back to $100. Investing $500 a month buys more units when prices are low, so $6,000 put in becomes about $8,456, up 41%, even though the price ended where it started. Halfway through, the same account was down about 30%: that is where many people stop.

This is an illustration with made-up prices, not real data and not a forecast. It only works if prices recover, which is not guaranteed: a single stock may never recover, and even broad markets can take years. Example: the S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 record close to its March 2009 low and only closed above that 2007 record in March 2013 (price index, dividends not included).

Source: Associated Press / NPR, "S&P 500 Closes At All-Time High, Rising Above Oct. 2007 Mark" (Mar 28, 2013): closes of 1,565.15 (Oct 9, 2007), 676.53 (Mar 9, 2009) and 1,569.19 (Mar 28, 2013).

Assumptions: $500 invested at the start of each month at that month's price, no fees or taxes. Past results don't guarantee future returns; prices can fall further and for longer. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: Say a fund drops from one hundred dollars to fifty, then climbs back.
Invest five hundred a month: five units at one hundred, ten at fifty.
So a crash is a sale. But here's the catch.

visual.label: price cut in half: twice as many units

scenes.say: Halfway, you're down almost thirty percent. Many people quit here.
Keep going, and six thousand becomes about eighty-four hundred fifty.
Real crashes run deep: the S and P five hundred once fell fifty-seven percent.
Its record took about five and a half years to return.
Here, buying through the drop made even a round trip pay.
